messages.author: 9b1ba46046eac99f
messages.subject: how to use Matt Trick for constrained variables?
parts:
Hi Stan,

I was trying to use Matt Trick for a constrained variable, but I am not sure how I could implement that...Could I have any suggestions? 

Say I want to have parameter theta to be bounded between -5 and 5, I could well constrain theta_mu, and explicitly constrain theta, but the theta support when 
using Matt Trick may cause theta go beyond the range. Possible I need to constrain theta_row with some math? 

parameter {
  real<lower=-5,upper=5> theta_mu;
  real<lower=0> theta_sd;
  real theta_row[N];  
}

transformed parameters {
   real<lower=-5,upper=5> theta[N];
   theta <- theta_mu + theta_sd * theta_row;
}

Thanks in advance,
Lei

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] how to use Matt Trick for constrained variables?
parts:
This isn't a non-centered parameterization (aka Matt trick) issue.
There's simply no way to constrain mu and sigma so that
normal(mu, sigma) falls in (-5,5). The best you can do is make it
unlikely that you fall out by taking mu in (-5,5) and taking sigma
small enough that it's unlikely to fall outside.

If you really need a value in (-5,5), you can scale and translate.

theta <- 10 * inv_logit(alpha) - 5;

This guarantees that theta is in (-5, 5) no matter what alpha is, so
you can have

for (n in 1:N)
theta[n] <- 10 * inv_logit(mu_theta + theta_raw * sigma_theta) - 5;

It's a different regression, though --- mu_thtea and sigma_theta now mean
something different.

- Bob

P.S. I think you meant theta_raw ("raw" as in uncooked).

messages.author: 0839befa8a8b7d53
messages.subject: Re: how to use Matt Trick for constrained variables?
parts:
Would it not work to just construct your bounded theta from a shifted and scaled inv_logit transform? Something like:

real theta[N];
theta <- inv_logit( theta_mu + theta_sd * theta_row )*10 - 5;

I don't know whether inv_logit is vectorized, so the above code may require a loop, but hopefully the idea comes across.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] how to use Matt Trick for constrained variables?
parts: If values below -5 and +5 hare hard to interpret, I expect that values such as -4.5 and +4.5 are somewhat hard to interpret, and values such as -5.5 and +5.5 are very hard to interpret. That is, I suspect a soft constraint is the way to go.  You’d still have prior information, just not a hard constraint.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: how to use Matt Trick for constrained variables?
parts:
Aside from the modeling issue, that statement will, perhaps
surprisingly, have absolutely no effect on sampling.

The problem is that it's branching on the value of a parameter,
then adding a constant to the log density. Constants added to
the log density never do anything to sampling. The log
density is either lp or lp + 1e-10, neither of which is an expression
involving theta. It got there via examining theta, but it has no way
of exploiting that discontinuity at theta = 5 or theta = -5.

- Bob

messages.author: 0839befa8a8b7d53
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] how to use Matt Trick for constrained variables?
parts:
A related issue here is how to apply soft constraints. I've previously imposed soft constraints in Stan by assigning a prior to the transformed parameter. For example, we often know a priori that log-odds of some event are not much below -5 and not much above +5. Applying regularization to the whole linear predictor seems a lot more natural at times than applying it to individual coefficients in the linear model.

If Andrew or anyone else has done some work on this issue, would be curious to read it.

I repeat that you should avoid hard constraints unless they are physically part of the problem.

How about?

if(theta < -5 || theta > 5)
   increment_log_prob(-1.0e10);

This would introduce a jump and probably make the solver unhappy.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] how to use Matt Trick for constrained variables?
parts:
If you apply a prior to a transformed parameter, be sure to
include the Jacobian.

Constraining the linear predictor can be viewed as a data-dependent
constraint on the coefficients. But I don't see how to make sense of
it from a modeling point of view.

If you really need to constrain the linear predictor to fall
in (-5, 5), then the scaled and shifted logit (or tanh) is one
way to do it.

Andrew at one point suggested using an IRT 3PL-like trick to
tame logistic regression in BUGS/JAGS, taking:

Pr[y[n] = 1] = 0.01 + 0.98 * inv_logit(alpha[n]);

where alpha[n] is the linear predictor for boolean observation y[n].
That guarantees the estimated probability stays in (0.01, 0.99). I
have no idea where to find that among Andrew's gazillion published
and unpublished papers, or even if I'm remembering entirely correctly.

- Bob

On Jul 6, 2015, at 3:10 PM, Richard McElreath <rmcel...@gmail.com> wrote:

A related issue here is how to apply soft constraints. I've previously imposed soft constraints in Stan by assigning a prior to the transformed parameter. For example, we often know a priori that log-odds of some event are not much below -5 and not much above +5. Applying regularization to the whole linear predictor seems a lot more natural at times than applying it to individual coefficients in the linear model.

If Andrew or anyone else has done some work on this issue, would be curious to read it.

On Sunday, July 5, 2015 at 3:45:51 PM UTC-7, Andrew Gelman wrote:
I repeat that you should avoid hard constraints unless they are physically part of the problem.

On Jul 5, 2015, at 6:22 AM, andre.p...@googlemail.com wrote:

How about?

if(theta < -5 || theta > 5)
   increment_log_prob(-1.0e10);

This would introduce a jump and probably make the solver unhappy.
